full_card.band: 8 h tier. Buckets: edits, EOL/BOM, line/offset queries, search, performance bounds. Frontier risk is CRLF splitting and large-file performance. Weaker model stops at plain string array. No dated public evidence of agent results, so Band capped at 3.
full_card.build_cost: About 3-4 days: isolate pieceTree and its deps from the trimmed snapshot, write the naive-oracle differential harness, calibrate perf thresholds, and make the suite deterministic with per-test reporting.
full_card.deliverable: Rebuilt piece-tree text buffer: red-black tree, line starts, CRLF/CR/LF normalisation, BOM handling, chunk builder, edits, offset/line queries, search, within large-file performance thresholds.
full_card.gates_anticheat: Hidden tests and config sealed outside /app; naive oracle not in image. Closes plain string-array backing via wall-clock large-file thresholds and call-count checks. Vendoring a newer copy is closed by history-less snapshot. Wrapping a system tool is not useful here.
full_card.grading_surface: Hidden randomised differential suite: random edit sequences compared against a naive string model for text, line and offset queries, EOL/BOM and search; plus node unit tests. Base fails all cases. Naive oracle gives an unlimited generator.
full_card.local_fit: Fits Node/CPU/8 cores/16 GB. Wall-clock perf thresholds on gVisor may be noisy; calibrate over several runs. Smoke build amber: exit-code-only report, zero listed tests, rc 1 on all three runs, so the offline unit runner needs isolating.

spike_plan.kill_if: Piece tree cannot be separated from the rest of the model layer without rewriting most of VS Code; or naive oracle disagrees with upstream on EOL/BOM in a way the spec cannot settle; or timings are too noisy to threshold.
spike_plan.pass_if: Dependency closure is isolable within a few thousand lines; naive model agrees with upstream on all queries for the seeded set; perf timings vary by under about 20% across runs; per-test reporting works offline.
steps: In a throwaway networked container, clone microsoft/vscode at tag 1.142.0 and confirm the four pieceTreeTextBuffer files are present.

Run npm ci offline-prep if needed, then run only the pieceTree and textModel mocha tests via --grep to get per-test pass/fail (the smoke run gave zero listed tests and rc 1 on all three runs, so check why).
Trim a copy: remove pieceTreeTextBuffer and list its imports from the rest of the model layer; record the dependency closure size in lines.
Write a naive string model (TextBuffer over a string) and a random edit generator with CRLF/CR/LF, BOM, insert/delete, line/offset and search queries.

Run the generator against the upstream pieceTreeTextBuffer for 1,000 seeded sequences and check the naive model agrees on every query; record any disagreements and whether they are spec-level or bugs.
Time build and edit on a generated 50-100 MB file over 3 runs each to see whether median wall-clock is stable enough for a threshold on gVisor.
Repeat the same seeds twice to check determinism.

v1.summary: The seed is real and licence-clean: the VS Code 1.142.0 tag, its piece-tree files and the MIT licence are all confirmed, and the grading surface (a naive-oracle differential suite) is large and sealable. Risks are that the piece tree is famous with a public MIT near-port (Seal 2, lookup partial), and that the smoke suite is amber, so the 8 h band and the perf thresholds still need a spike before a frontier band claim can stand.
